prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry based on reversible terminators and clonally amplified clusters

statement.case_for: Sequencing-by-synthesis is molecular design in the sense I value most: reversible terminators, fluorescent nucleotide chemistry and surface-clustered single-molecule templates were engineered so that a chemical reaction becomes a digital readout. It changed what researchers and clinicians can actually do, from routine whole-genome and tumour sequencing to infectious-disease surveillance and population-scale biology. Four of eight members placed it in their top two, and the opening ballots show that support comes from very different scientific viewpoints (biophysical chemistry, enzymology, simulation and materials), which suggests it is not a taste of any one subfield. The work is two decades old and independently confirmed, so recognition is overdue. The Cambridge pair is the cleanest attribution because they conceived and built the integrated chemistry and the platform around it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that sequencing already has a Chemistry prize (Sanger and Gilbert, 1980), so a sceptic can call this a scale-up of a known capability, and some will see it as a tool for biology and medicine more than a chemical discovery. Attribution is also genuinely contested: Mayer (clonal colony amplification), Ju (alternative terminator chemistry) and Rothberg (pyrosequencing and semiconductor sequencing) all have claims, and a prize restricted to two or three names will exclude real contributors. I cannot verify the detailed priority and patent history from the shortlist alone.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B017 first and proposes adding Pascal Mayer to Balasubramanian and Klenerman, crediting his clustering and colony amplification as part of the core chemistry.
responses.response: I take the Mayer argument seriously, because clonal amplification on a surface is what made the reversible-terminator chemistry scalable. My hesitation is that Mayer's contribution is a concept and amplification route, while the Cambridge pair delivered the integrated terminator chemistry and a working single-molecule and cluster platform. I would keep two names as my preferred configuration but would not oppose a third seat for Mayer if the expert reports show the cluster idea was decisive and not just parallel, and I think we should settle this in round 2 rather than in the citation wording.

responses.point: Linke, our chair, ranks halide perovskite absorbers first for a clear physical principle and new capability, and puts sequencing second, while worrying about crowded credit among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Seok, Gratzel and Kanatzidis.
responses.response: I agree that perovskites are a vivid case of a simple principle producing a new capability, and the efficiency trajectory is remarkable. I would qualify it on two grounds: the credit is as crowded as Linke says, and long-term stability and lead content are unresolved, so the technology has not yet delivered at scale in the way sequencing has. Sequencing has two decades of use behind it and a clearer two-person core, so I would put maturity and attribution clarity ahead of novelty of principle here. I do not think perovskites are a poor candidate, only a later one.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling first, arguing that Buchwald and Hartwig turned aryl amine construction into a routine operation, with a clean two-person attribution and complementarity to the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
responses.response: Somfai's attribution argument is the strongest of any candidate on the list, and I accept that the method changed everyday synthetic practice. Where I differ is on the size of the conceptual step: the 2010 prize already recognised the Pd cross-coupling framework, and the C-N extension, although enormously useful, is an expansion of that framework, whereas sequencing created a capability that did not exist at scale. I would keep B048 as a serious alternative, and I would be persuaded if colleagues think the ligand-design principle is a distinct concept and not an extension.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular phase separation first as a new physical-chemical concept of cellular organisation, with Hyman and Brangwynne as the founding observation and Rosen as the quantitative framework.
responses.response: I ranked B029 fourth and agree that it introduced phase-behaviour thinking into cell biology. My reservation is that the active debate over which cellular structures are truly phase-separated, and the still limited therapeutic or technological consequences, make it less settled than the sequencing work. I also want to flag that Pappu and Mittag are excluded from a three-person cut, and I would want that attribution question resolved before this is a prize candidate. I would welcome more discussion of how much of the field is robust.

responses.point: Chabes ranks sequencing first with the Cambridge pair, and emphasises that its impact on genome biology is lasting while admitting uncertainty about the decisive split among five credited people.
responses.response: We agree on the core configuration, and I think that shared uncertainty about Mayer, Ju and Rothberg is the correct place to focus. Chabes asks whether the committee would treat this as chemistry or as a biology tool. I think the reversible-terminator and fluorescent-nucleotide chemistry makes the answer chemistry, and the citation should say so explicitly to avoid the impression of a medicine prize.

uncertainties: Whether to add Pascal Mayer as a third laureate for clonal amplification, and how to treat Ju and Rothberg's competing routes.
Whether colleagues who ranked sequencing low (Brzezinski, Sparr, Somfai and Zou did not rank it in their top eight) see it as a tool for biology rather than a chemical discovery.
Whether a second prize part, such as targeted protein degradation, is worth discussing despite the lack of an approved degrader drug and the difficulty of selecting three of eight credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. Candidates for sequencing, degraders, base editing and phase separation have no direct link to my postdoc mentors Molly Stevens or Freddy Boey or to Linkoping colleagues. My research overlap with Emma Sparr on self-assembly is a scientific proximity, not a recusal issue.
